newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian space station, cargo craft collide.
newsitem.headline: Russian space station, cargo craft collide.

text.p: Russia's Mir space station hit a cargo craft during a manual docking exercise on Wednesday but there was no immediate danger to the U.S. astronaut and two Russians on board, mission control said.

A spokeswoman for the mission control centre near Moscow said the unmanned Progress cargo craft collided at 1.20 p.m. (0920 GMT) with the Spektr scientific module attached to the main section of Mir, causing a partial loss of air pressure.
Mir is manned by U.S. astronaut Michael Foale, who reached the station on the space shuttle Atlantis in May and was to stay until September, and Russians Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin.
A spokesman for the U.S space agency NASA said earlier on Wednesday that the crew had been able to seal off the damaged compartment after the collision.
"The crew said the air pressure on the station was normal and there is no immediate danger," the Russian spokeswoman said by telephone.
She said the main part of the station -- in orbit for more than a decade -- was not affected by the collision but added that a solar battery on the Spektr may have been damaged.
The spokeswoman said the crew was in the main section of Mir during the collision. NASA officials said Foale's living quarters were in the damaged Spektr unit.

It was not clear what effect the collision would have on the mission. A space expert who requested anonymity said damage to the solar battery could cause serious problems but declined to give details until the full picture emerged.
RIA news agency quoted space experts as saying that the Spektr, one of Mir's eight modules, is the main carrier of solar batteries and the chief source of energy for the entire station.

The ageing Mir was launched in 1986. It is due to be replaced by an international station in the next few years. Mir has suffered a series of malfunctions in recent months -- in February, a fire broke out, followed by a leak of coolant.
Malfunctions during automatic dockings have become a recurrent problem, and Wednesday's manual docking was part of a training programme to help the crew cope with them.

"Cargo craft are normally docked in automatic mode but because of a string of recent failures the cosmonauts train in manual docking from time to time to polish their skills," the Russian spokeswoman said.
She said the Progress craft, weighing about 15,430 lb (7,000 kg), had been uncoupled from Mir on Tuesday to be manually re-docked after nearly 24 hours of free flight.
The spokeswoman could not say what exactly caused the collision and who was in charge of the manual docking.
The crew could be returned to Earth at short notice in a Russian Soyuz escape craft kept docked to Mir at all times. NASA officials said there was no immediate plan to evacuate the three men.
